slides.title: Cover Slide/Main Slide
slides.speaker: Aryanraj S Singh
slides.script: Good morning. We are Team 10. Our project is plant disease detection using a pretrained CNN, tuned with Differential Evolution. In simple words, we used an evolution-inspired search to find better training settings for a tomato leaf disease classifier. Our guide is Manoj Kumar S, Assistant Professor.

slides.title: Introduction to Optimization Problems
slides.speaker: Aryanraj S Singh
slides.script: Optimization means finding the settings that give the best result. Our model has seven training settings, such as how fast it learns and how much of the network we retrain. To score one set of settings, we train a model and test it on images it has not seen. With a fixed number of tries, we want the best settings.

slides.title: What are Nature-Inspired Algorithms?
slides.speaker: Aryanraj S Singh
slides.script: Nature-inspired algorithms borrow ideas from nature to search for good solutions. They keep a population, a group of candidate solutions. They create new candidates by mixing and changing old ones, like offspring. And they keep whichever candidate scores better, like survival of the fittest.

slides.title: Classification of Nature-Inspired Algorithms
slides.speaker: Aryanraj S Singh
slides.script:
These methods come in a few families. Evolutionary methods include the Genetic Algorithm and Differential Evolution. Swarm methods include Particle Swarm and Ant Colony. Others include Simulated Annealing. We chose Differential Evolution, or DE, because it is simple, has few settings of its own, and works well on problems like ours.

Handoff: “Richik will now explain our problem and data.”

slides.title: Problem Statement
slides.speaker: Richik Chaudhuri
slides.script: Tomato leaf diseases cause big crop losses, and experts are not always available. Our goal is to let DE pick the training settings that best detect these diseases. We use the PlantVillage tomato images: 18,146 photos in ten classes, nine diseases plus healthy. We split them into 70% for training, 15% for validation and 15% for the final test.

slides.title: Implementation and Results (1/10)
slides.speaker: Richik Chaudhuri
slides.script: This is our full system. We clean the images and split them. We train a standard baseline. Then DE and random search each look for better settings using the validation images. The best recipes are trained three times, and only then do we score them on the test images. Finally, the models power our offline demo.

slides.title: Implementation and Results (2/10)
slides.speaker: Richik Chaudhuri
slides.script:
Our model is EfficientNet-B0, a compact image network already trained on over a million everyday photos (ImageNet). We reuse that knowledge and add a small classification layer for our ten classes. The baseline is a standard, common recipe: it keeps the pretrained part frozen and trains only the last layer. We fixed it before any search began.

Handoff: “Suraj will explain how DE works.”

slides.title: Implementation and Results (3/10)
slides.speaker: Suraj B
slides.script: DE improves a group of candidate settings, generation by generation. First, mutation: it takes three other candidates and adds the difference between two of them to the third, giving a new direction to try. Second, crossover: it blends this new candidate with the current one, setting by setting. Third, selection: we train both and keep the one with the better validation score. We wrote all of this ourselves in NumPy and tested every step.

slides.title: Implementation and Results (4/10)
slides.speaker: Suraj B
slides.script: These are the seven settings DE tunes. Some control learning, like the learning rate. Some prevent overfitting, like dropout and weight decay. Two control the network itself: the size of the final layer and how many blocks of the pretrained network we retrain. DE used 8 candidates over 8 generations, 72 training runs, and random search got exactly the same 72.

slides.title: Implementation and Results (5/10)
slides.speaker: Suraj B
slides.script: Here is the search itself. The line shows the best validation score found so far. Random search is a strong, fair control: it tries random settings with the same budget. DE climbs steadily and ends with the best search score, 97.07% against 96.36% for random search.

slides.title: Implementation and Results (6/10)
slides.speaker: Suraj B
slides.script:
This is our main result. Averaged over three training runs, the baseline reaches 97.43% accuracy. The DE recipe reaches 99.85%. Macro-F1, the average score across all ten classes, rises from 96.60% to 99.80%. That means DE removes about 94% of the baseline’s mistakes. Random search also reaches 99.85%, so DE matches a strong equal-budget control.

Handoff: “Sushant will show where the improvements come from.”

slides.title: Implementation and Results (7/10)
slides.speaker: Sushant Deo
slides.script: These grids show where mistakes go. Each row is the true disease and each column is the prediction, so a dark diagonal means correct answers. The baseline mixes up several diseases, for example Target Spot with spider mites. With DE, almost every image lands on the diagonal.

slides.title: Implementation and Results (8/10)
slides.speaker: Sushant Deo
slides.script: Here we look at each disease separately. Every one of the ten classes improves with DE. The biggest gains are on Early blight and Target Spot, about 6.8 points each, which were the hardest classes for the baseline.

slides.title: Implementation and Results (9/10)
slides.speaker: Sushant Deo
slides.script: Grad-CAM is a heatmap that shows where the model looked when it made its decision. Warm colours mean more attention. Both models classify these leaves correctly, and the DE model spreads its attention across the leaf itself rather than the edges or background.

slides.title: Implementation and Results (10/10)
slides.speaker: Sushant Deo
slides.script: So what did DE actually learn? The biggest change is that it chose to retrain all nine blocks of the pretrained network instead of keeping them frozen. It also picked a slightly higher learning rate and added label smoothing, which keeps the model from being over-confident. This is a clear, useful finding about how to fine-tune.

slides.title: Live Demo
slides.speaker: Sushant Deo
slides.script:
First 25 seconds: Open the demo at http://127.0.0.1:8000, press P for presentation mode, pick a sample tomato leaf and click analyze. Point to the two predictions side by side, the top-3 probabilities, and the Grad-CAM heatmaps.

Next 15 seconds: Apply a mild blur and analyze again, and describe how the scores change.

Final 20 seconds: Open Evolution Lab, pick Rastrigin and press run. Press Space to pause and explain: each dot is a candidate, and the group moves toward the lowest point. Then return to the slides.

If the demo cannot start, play demo/demo.gif, the recording of the same demo.

slides.title: Performance Metrics and Benchmarking (1/5)
slides.speaker: Sushant Deo
slides.script: We use three simple scores. Accuracy is the share of test images labelled correctly. Macro-F1 averages the score across all ten classes, so a rare disease counts as much as a common one. ROC-AUC tells us how well the model ranks the right disease above the wrong ones, where 1.0 is perfect.

slides.title: Performance Metrics and Benchmarking (2/5)
slides.speaker: Sushant Deo
slides.script:
Is the gain real? The table shows the likely range of each score, from a thousand resamples of the test set. The DE range sits well above the baseline range. On the same test images, DE fixes 60 baseline mistakes, while the baseline is right on only 3 that DE misses. The McNemar test confirms this is not due to chance: p is about 9.05 times ten to the minus 15, far below 0.001.

Handoff: “Richik will show how DE performs on its own.”

slides.title: Performance Metrics and Benchmarking (3/5)
slides.speaker: Richik Chaudhuri
slides.script: To check that our DE code works well by itself, we also tested it on five standard math test functions, separate from the CNN. We compared DE with an adaptive DE called jDE, the Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm and random search. Each method had 30 runs with 20,000 tries per run, and lower error is better.

slides.title: Performance Metrics and Benchmarking (4/5)
slides.speaker: Richik Chaudhuri
slides.script: This table shows the typical final error. DE beats random search on all five functions and is the best method on Rosenbrock, a famously tricky valley-shaped function. Other methods win on other functions, which is normal: each method has its strengths.

slides.title: Performance Metrics and Benchmarking (5/5)
slides.speaker: Richik Chaudhuri
slides.script: Here is the cost. Training the DE recipe three times took 84.5 minutes, compared with 30.5 for the baseline, because DE retrains the whole network. The search itself took about 46 minutes. Once trained, all three models answer in under 5 milliseconds per image and have a similar size.

slides.title: Advantages and Limitations
slides.speaker: Aryanraj S Singh
slides.script: To sum up our strengths: accuracy rose from 97.43% to 99.85%, our DE is written from scratch and tested, the comparison is fair with equal budgets, and everything runs offline on a laptop. The main limitations are that PlantVillage photos are taken in a lab, we cover one crop, and the search needs extra training time.

slides.title: Future Scope
slides.speaker: Suraj B
slides.script: Next, we want to test on real farm photos taken with phones. We also plan a multi-objective DE, which would reward not just accuracy but also robustness to blur and noise, reliable confidence and speed. Finally, we would like an on-device mobile app and self-tuning DE variants such as SHADE.
